convention: All sky images are equirectangular (plate carree, CAR) all-sky maps in ICRS (J2000) equatorial coordinates with width W = 2 x height H. Pixel column x (0-based) has its centre at RA = 360*(x+0.5)/W degrees: RA increases to the RIGHT in the stored image and RA = 0 h lies on the left edge (RA = 360 on the right edge). Pixel row y (0-based from the top) has its centre at Dec = 90 - 180*(y+0.5)/H degrees: north celestial pole along the top edge, south celestial pole along the bottom. This is the view of the celestial sphere from OUTSIDE (like a globe texture); as seen from inside the sphere (the real sky), east is to the left, so a sky-sphere renderer must mirror the texture horizontally (or map it onto the inside of the sphere with u = RA/360 increasing eastward). Direction for a pixel: v = (cos Dec cos RA, cos Dec sin RA, sin Dec) in ICRS. Landmarks: Galactic Centre (RA 266.40, Dec -28.94) at x/W = 0.740, y/H = 0.661; LMC (RA 80.9, Dec -69.8) at x/W = 0.225, y/H = 0.888; Orion Nebula (RA 83.8, Dec -5.4) at x/W = 0.233, y/H = 0.530.

bands.reveals: This is starlight: the summed light of about 1.8 billion stars measured by ESA's Gaia satellite in its blue, green and red passbands. The bright band is the disc of our own Milky Way seen edge-on from inside it, and the dark, reddened lanes are clouds of interstellar dust that absorb and redden the light of the stars behind them. The two smudges in the far south are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, satellite galaxies about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years away.
caveats: Built from the Gaia DR3 source catalogue, not from a photograph: diffuse glowing gas (e.g. the Orion Nebula) is absent, and stars brighter than about G = 3 mag are missing or incomplete in Gaia.
Faint stripes from Gaia's scanning pattern and star-count noise are visible in low-density regions at full resolution.
Cosmos applied a per-channel levels curve (black point 40/255, gamma 1.6) to the CDS colour composite to obtain a dark sky background.

bands.reveals: Hydrogen-alpha is deep-red light emitted when electrons recombine with protons in hydrogen gas that has been ionized by the ultraviolet light of hot young stars or by shock waves. It lights up glowing H II regions such as the Orion–Eridanus bubble with Barnard's Loop and the giant Gum Nebula, plus a faint "warm ionized medium" that fills the Galactic disc.
caveats: Composite of three surveys with different resolutions (WHAM ~1°, VTSS/SHASSA ~6′); regions covered only by WHAM look smoother.
Not corrected for dust extinction: Hα from distant regions of the Galactic plane (e.g. towards the Galactic Centre) is strongly dimmed.
Residual artifacts around some bright stars may be visible.

bands.reveals: Near-infrared light passes through interstellar dust far more easily than visible light (about ten times less dimming at 2.2 µm), so the dense star clouds of the Galactic bulge and disc that are hidden in the visible view shine through. Most of this light comes from cool, old red-giant stars, which trace where most of the Milky Way's stellar mass is.
caveats: Mosaic of 2MASS Atlas tiles: faint seams between tiles and saturated halos around the brightest stars are possible.

bands.reveals: Ultraviolet light is emitted mostly by hot, massive, short-lived young stars and by hot white dwarfs, so it pinpoints recent star formation in nearby galaxies and the hottest stars in our own. Dust absorbs ultraviolet light very strongly, which is one reason the dusty Galactic plane looks dark here.
caveats: Partial sky (~79%): the Galactic plane, the Magellanic Clouds and fields around very bright stars were mostly avoided to protect the detectors; no-data areas are black and flagged in the mask file.
Where only near-UV data exist (the far-UV detector failed in 2009) the colour is reddish.

bands.reveals: Soft X-rays come from gas heated to millions of degrees: the expanding shells of supernova remnants such as Vela and the Cygnus Loop, the hot "Local Bubble" that surrounds the Sun, superheated gas in clusters of galaxies, and matter falling onto black holes in distant active galaxies. Red marks the very softest X-rays (0.1–0.4 keV), which are absorbed even by thin clouds of gas; blue marks harder X-rays (0.5–2.4 keV) that travel farther.
caveats: Counts-based maps (Poisson noise) at about 2′ native resolution, shown smoothed by resampling; the all-sky survey has strong exposure/scan artefacts: bright fan-shaped streaks converge on the ecliptic poles and dark gaps appear where exposure was low (these are instrumental, not sky structure); soft X-rays are absorbed by neutral Galactic gas, which suppresses the low-energy (red) channel along the plane, so colours are orange/blue rather than uniformly dark.

bands.reveals: eROSITA mapped the X-ray sky far more sensitively than ROSAT. It reveals the "eROSITA bubbles" — enormous lobes of million-degree gas blown out of the centre of the Milky Way — along with supernova remnants, hot galaxy clusters and hundreds of thousands of growing supermassive black holes.
caveats: Only the western Galactic hemisphere (Galactic longitude 180°–360°, the eROSITA-DE share) is public; the other half of the sky is black (no data) and flagged in the mask file.

bands.reveals: Gamma rays are the most energetic light. The glowing Galactic plane is made by cosmic rays — particles accelerated by exploding stars — smashing into interstellar gas, while the bright dots are pulsars (spinning neutron stars such as Vela, Geminga and the Crab) and blazars: galaxies whose supermassive black holes fire jets almost straight at us.
caveats: Angular resolution depends strongly on energy (about 1° near 300 MeV, ~0.1° above 10 GeV); faint sources look blurred.

Away from the Galactic plane the mottled blue-grey pattern is the Cosmic Microwave Background itself shining through.
caveats: Angular resolution 13′–33′ depending on frequency; the composite colour scale was chosen by CDS.

bands.reveals: The Cosmic Microwave Background is the oldest light in the Universe, released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang when the cooling Universe first became transparent. Its temperature is 2.7255 K in every direction to about one part in 100,000; the colours show those tiny differences (blue colder, red warmer, by up to about ±300 µK), the seeds from which galaxies and galaxy clusters later grew.
caveats: Foreground-cleaned with the SMICA method; residual Galactic emission and point sources remain in a thin strip along the Galactic plane.
The monopole (2.7255 K) and the dipole due to the Sun's motion (±3.36 mK) are removed; values are temperature differences in µK (K_CMB units).
Effective resolution 5′ FWHM.

Giant arcs such as the North Polar Spur (Loop I) are the shells of ancient supernova explosions and stellar winds, and the brightest regions trace the spiral arms and the Galactic Centre.
caveats: Low angular resolution (≈56′ FWHM); bright compact radio sources have been subtracted in this reprocessed version.

bands.reveals: Cold and warm neutral hydrogen atoms emit radio waves at exactly 21 cm. This map shows how many hydrogen atoms lie along each line of sight: the thick gas disc of the Milky Way, gas clouds falling onto the Galaxy, and the Magellanic Stream — a trail of gas torn from the Magellanic Clouds.
caveats: Angular resolution 16.2′; column densities assume optically thin emission (underestimated in the densest clouds).
